content: The determination of hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA levels is critical for assessing whether the disease is inactive or requires treatment. These levels are also used to monitor the effectiveness of antiviral therapy, as an increase in HBV DNA may indicate the emergence of drug-resistant viral variants. The World Health Organization (WHO) has standardized the expression of HBV DNA concentrations, with specific equivalencies such as 10,000 copies/mL equating to 2,000 IU/mL. It is recommended to use the same assay consistently for a single patient to evaluate treatment efficacy. However, access to HBV DNA testing remains limited in resource-constrained settings. A comprehensive assessment of liver disease severity includes clinical evaluation for signs of cirrhosis and decompensation, as well as laboratory tests such as serum bilirubin, albumin, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and prothrombin time. A complete blood count, including platelet count, is also essential. Typically, ALT levels are higher than AST levels, but this ratio may reverse as cirrhosis progresses. Markers of liver synthetic function and portal hypertension, such as serum albumin, bilirubin, platelet count, and prothrombin time, are also critical. A decline in albumin, an increase in bilirubin, and prolonged prothrombin time are characteristic of decompensated cirrhosis. Liver biopsy has traditionally been used to evaluate the degree of necroinflammation and fibrosis, aiding treatment decisions. However, biopsies have limitations, including sampling error, subjectivity in interpretation, high costs, risks of complications (e.g., bleeding, pneumothorax), patient discomfort, and the need for specialized training and infrastructure, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Non-invasive tests (NITs) are increasingly replacing liver biopsy for staging liver disease in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) patients. Blood-based markers such as the AST-to-platelet ratio index (APRI) and FIB-4, as well as commercial tests like FibroTest, can estimate fibrosis. Transient elastography (FibroScan) is another non-invasive method used to rule out advanced fibrosis. These methods have been validated in adults with CHB and are particularly useful in resource-limited settings. Screening for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is recommended for high-risk groups, including household and sexual contacts of CHB patients, individuals with HIV, people who inject drugs (PWID), men who have sex with men, sex workers, indigenous populations, incarcerated individuals, and transgender persons. Blood and organ donors should also be screened to prevent HBV transmission. In the United States and Europe, population-based screening is recommended for migrants from HBV-endemic regions. However, there is limited guidance on HBsAg screening in LMICs. WHO is developing consolidated guidelines for hepatitis B and C testing and management. Prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HBV is highly effective with the use of recombinant DNA-derived vaccines. Administering the first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth, followed by at least two additional doses, is 90–95% effective in preventing HBV infection. Universal infant vaccination has significantly reduced CHB prevalence among children in regions with established programs. However, a small proportion of vaccinated children (5–10%) may have a poor response to the vaccine and remain susceptible to HBV infection as adults. In countries with intermediate or low HBV endemicity, a substantial disease burden arises from infections acquired during adolescence or adulthood. Catch-up vaccination programs targeting adolescents and high-risk groups, such as PWID and individuals with multiple sexual partners, are essential. Antiviral therapy is crucial for individuals with CHB at high risk of disease progression to reduce morbidity. Over the past three decades, treatment outcomes have improved with the introduction of nucleos(t)ide analogues (NAs) and pegylated interferon (PEG-IFN). While NAs effectively suppress HBV replication, they rarely result in a cure, necessitating long-term or lifelong therapy. NAs are preferred over interferon due to their fewer side effects and convenient oral administration. However, interferon has advantages such as the absence of resistance and higher rates of HBeAg and HBsAg loss, though it is less effective overall and associated with significant side effects, high costs, and limited use in resource-limited settings. Contraindications to interferon include decompensated cirrhosis, autoimmune diseases, pregnancy, and certain comorbidities. Emerging therapies, such as tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF), offer enhanced delivery of active metabolites to hepatocytes, reducing toxicity. Research is ongoing to develop curative strategies targeting all replicative forms of HBV, including covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA). Novel approaches include entry inhibitors, short-interfering RNAs (siRNAs), capsid inhibitors, and immunotherapeutic strategies to enhance HBV-specific immune responses. Coinfections with HBV, HIV, HCV, or HDV often result in more severe liver disease and higher rates of cirrhosis, HCC, and mortality. HIV coinfection accelerates HBV disease progression and reduces treatment response. HDV, a defective RNA virus requiring HBV for replication, is associated with more severe liver disease and accelerated progression to cirrhosis. Vaccination against HBV prevents HDV coinfection. HCV coinfection is common in HBV-endemic regions and increases the risk of HCC. Management of HCV infection is detailed in WHO guidelines. In children, CHB is often asymptomatic and in the immune-tolerant phase. Treatment is generally not recommended for those with minimal histological disease due to low immediate risk of progression and concerns about long-term safety and drug resistance. However, children with severe necroinflammatory disease or cirrhosis may require antiviral therapy. Tenofovir and entecavir are approved for use in children and adolescents. Non-invasive methods, such as APRI and FibroScan, are recommended for assessing liver fibrosis and cirrhosis in resource-limited settings. These tests are cost-effective, require minimal expertise, and can be performed in outpatient settings. Transient elastography, while effective, is limited by high equipment costs and the need for maintenance and trained operators. Accurate and validated NITs can optimize the selection of CHB patients for antiviral therapy, reducing the reliance on liver biopsy.
